doc.title: Alan Broadbent interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 26, 2023

chapter: New Zealand and the road to jazz
title: Auckland pop radio, a first jazz group and New Zealand pianists
summary: He describes the English pop on local radio, answering an ad to form a group with bass and drums, and meeting older musicians such as Dave McRae and Mike Nock.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: If you turned on your favorite radio station at the time, it probably would have been AM, what kind of music were you likely to hear in Auckland at that time, early ‘60s?

I think you would have heard the pop music of England and that would have been The Beatles and all that was starting to happen, The Stones. And just before that there were Tommy Steele, there were these English artists who went on to do Finian’s Rainbow I think, Tommy Steele was a big rock star in England, people like that, Gene Pitney — he was American with the “Town Without Pity” or something like that.
Yeah. Did you ever put on — have the record player near the piano and put on recordings and try to poke along and see what was going on?

No I didn’t have the means to do that at the time. But I knew intuitively how to do it and I answered an ad of some like-minded kids that wanted to form a group and that was my first time with a bass player, drummer, and we were all trying to create this feeling, you know, of thousands of miles away from where it really was happening, and I had to find a way to get over the ocean and experience it.
Well said. Did it take you time or did you figure out on your own what C 7 and F major 7 and all those symbols meant?

Yeah I figured all that out. But then as I was meeting friends who were musicians and I met some serious older musicians who had been playing in Sydney and they were like, one of them an absolutely great jazz pianist, Dave McRae. Dave became, through a chain of circumstances, Buddy Rich’s piano player in the ‘70s and Buddy’s favorite pianist. Dave could groove like mad. But I think he’s retired from all of that. So there were these — Mike Nock is another pretty famous New Zealander but he went in the (whatever you want to call it) jazz fusion thing that lost that feeling for me that I was interested in. Not that I don’t admire the music or anything but I’ve always wanted that feeling. Otherwise I’ll go and listen to an 80-piece orchestra you know. © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-
